# Question

**Which is better for peak performance: a short mild warm-up or a long intense warm-up?** Neiva et al. (2015, *J Strength Cond Res*) had 11 elite swimmers complete a randomized crossover of a 600 m (short, mild) vs 1,800 m (long, intense) warm-up before 100 m time trials.

## Data source

Reconstruction of the published group means/SDs (n = 11; SWU 59.38 ± 2.18 s, LWU 60.18 ± 2.46 s). Within-swimmer pairing assumed r = 0.50, with a documented sensitivity analysis across r = 0.3–0.9.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Individual 100 m times under each warm-up (grey: swimmers; colour: means)"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
for _, r in df.iterrows():
    ax.plot([0, 1], [r["swu_100m_s"], r["lwu_100m_s"]],
            marker="o", color="grey", alpha=0.45, lw=0.9)
ax.plot([0, 1], [df["swu_100m_s"].mean()] * 2, marker="o", lw=3,
        color="#8fbf8f", label="mean (short mild)")
ax.plot([0, 1], [df["lwu_100m_s"].mean()] * 2, marker="o", lw=3,
        color="#c76c6c", label="mean (long intense)")
ax.set_xticks([0, 1], ["Short mild\n(600 m)", "Long intense\n(1,800 m)"])
ax.set_ylabel("100 m time (s)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Paired t-test (pairing assumption r = 0.5), sign-flip randomization (100k), bootstrap CI of the mean difference, plus Welch unpaired test and a pairing-correlation sensitivity analysis.

| Method | Result |
|---|---|
| Mean 100 m time | 59.38 s (SWU) vs 60.18 s (LWU), diff = −0.80 s |
| Paired t (r = 0.5 assumption) | t(10) = −1.14, p = 0.282 |
| Sign-flip randomization | p = 0.282 |
| Bootstrap 95% CI | (−2.13, +0.48) s |
| Welch (unpaired) | t = −0.81, p = 0.429 |
| Sensitivity (r = 0.9) | p = 0.033 |

# Decision

**Not significant at the assumed pairing.** With n = 11 the study cannot rule out a meaningful effect; the direction favours the short mild warm-up, consistent with the paper's caution that a long intense warm-up *may* impair 100 m performance. Only under near-perfect pairing (r = 0.9) would significance emerge — an honest example of small-sample ambiguity.
